about: Synthetic six-month journal of a final-year CS student, written for this project. Assumptions, verdicts and evidence are hand-labeled. It seeds the demo workspace and is the gold set for backend/evals. Every evidence string is an exact quote from its outcome text. 'theme' groups related decisions and is the ground truth for the retrieval eval.

decisions.title: Learn React in two weeks for the hackathon
decisions.reasoning: The hackathon is in 16 days and our team needs a frontend. I think two weeks of evenings is enough to learn React if I go straight to hooks. My JavaScript is solid, so I can skip the fundamentals. The official tutorial and a couple of YouTube courses should cover everything our project needs.
decisions.alternatives: Use plain HTML with a CSS framework, or let a teammate own the frontend.
decisions.expected_outcome: I build the hackathon frontend in React myself.
decisions.premortem: It's review day and this failed because the two weeks of evenings never really existed once coursework showed up.
missing_considerations: How many evenings are actually free during assignment weeks
A fallback if React isn't ready in time

assumptions.text: Two weeks of evenings is enough to learn React
assumptions.evidence: assignments ate most of my evenings

assumptions.text: My JavaScript is strong enough to skip the fundamentals
assumptions.evidence: The JavaScript side was fine

assumptions.text: Tutorials will cover what our project needs

outcome.what_happened: I got through components and hooks, but state management took most of the second week and assignments ate most of my evenings. The JavaScript side was fine. For the hackathon we used a UI template and I only wired up two screens.
outcome.lesson: Budget learning time against the evenings you really have; assignments always take a share.

decisions.title: Apply to 30 internships with one generic resume
decisions.reasoning: Internship season is short, so I want to maximize applications. I think volume matters more than tailoring at this stage, since most companies just skim resumes. If I send 30 applications this week, recruiters should get back to me within two weeks and I'll have a few interviews lined up.
decisions.alternatives: Tailor resumes for 8 to 10 roles I actually want.
decisions.expected_outcome: Get at least two interview calls within three weeks.
decisions.premortem: It's review day and this failed because a generic resume looked generic to every recruiter.
missing_considerations: What reply rate generic applications usually get
Whether the resume matches each role

assumptions.text: Volume matters more than tailoring
assumptions.evidence: the resume didn't match the roles

assumptions.text: Recruiters will reply within two weeks
assumptions.evidence: 3 replies out of 30

outcome.what_happened: 3 replies out of 30 after three weeks, all rejections. Two seniors who looked at it said the resume didn't match the roles I applied for.
outcome.lesson: Ten tailored applications beat thirty generic ones; track reply rate, not volume.

decisions.title: Launch my habit-tracker app in one month
decisions.reasoning: I've wanted a portfolio project that people actually use. One month is enough to build and launch a simple habit tracker if I work on it every day. My friends said they'd try it, so I'll get feedback quickly. I don't need a backend for the first version since everything can live in local storage.
decisions.alternatives: Contribute to an existing open-source habit app.
decisions.expected_outcome: The app is live with at least 10 people using it weekly.
decisions.premortem: It's review day and this failed because the one-month plan had no buffer and nobody committed to using it.
missing_considerations: How users will find the app beyond friends
What happens if it slips past a month

assumptions.text: One month is enough to build and launch the app
assumptions.evidence: Launch took seven weeks

assumptions.text: Friends will try it and give feedback
assumptions.evidence: Two friends signed up and never opened it again

assumptions.text: I won't need a backend for the first version
assumptions.evidence: I ended up needing a backend for sync anyway

outcome.what_happened: Launch took seven weeks, not four. Two friends signed up and never opened it again. Everyone wanted their habits on both phone and laptop, so I ended up needing a backend for sync anyway.
outcome.lesson: Ask users what they need before deciding what the first version can skip.
